name: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
credit: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, 19th-century photograph · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay (1838–1894) was a Bengali novelist, essayist and poet, and a deputy magistrate in the British Indian civil service for over thirty years. Educated at Presidency College, Calcutta, he was among the first graduates of the University of Calcutta, and he is regarded as the founder of the modern Bengali novel, with Durgeshnandini (1865), Kapalkundala (1866), Bishabriksha (1873) and the journal Bangadarshan (from 1872).

His song 'Vande Mataram', written about 1875 in a Sanskritised Bengali, was printed in his novel Anandamath (1882), where it is sung by the sannyasi rebels of the story. It became a rallying cry of the Indian nationalist movement and was later adopted as India's national song. This archive gives the song as printed in Anandamath, with Aurobindo Ghose's English verse translation of 1909.

poems.title: বন্দে মাতরম্ (Vande Mataram)
poems.author: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
poems.note: The song as sung in Chapter 10 of Book 1 of the novel Anandamath; the English verse translation by Aurobindo Ghose follows as the next poem.
poems.text:
বন্দে মাতরম্।
সুজলাং সুফলাং
মলয়জশীতলাং
শস্যশ্যামলাং
মাতরম্।

শুভ্র-জ্যোৎস্না-পুলকিত-যামিনীম্
ফুল্লকুসুমিত-দ্রুমদলশোভিনীম্,
সুহাসিনীং সুমধুরভাষিণীম্
সুখদাং বরদাং মাতরম্॥

সপ্তকোটীকণ্ঠকলকলনিনাদকরালে
দ্বিসপ্তকোটীভুজৈর্ধৃতখর-করবালে,
অবলা কেন মা এত বলে।
বহুবলধারিণীং
নমামি তারিণীং
রিপুদলবারিণীং
মাতরম্।

তুমি বিদ্যা তুমি ধর্ম
তুমি হৃদি তুমি মর্ম
ত্বং হি প্রাণাঃ শরীরে।
বাহুতে তুমি মা শক্তি
হৃদয়ে তুমি মা ভক্তি
তোমারই প্রতিমা গড়ি
মন্দিরে মন্দিরে।

ত্বং হি দুর্গা দশপ্রহরণধারিণী
কমলা কমল-দলবিহারিণী
বাণী বিদ্যাদায়িনী
নমামি ত্বাং
নমামি কমলাম্
অমলাং অতুলাম্
সুজলাং সুফলাম্
মাতরম্

বন্দে মাতরম্
শ্যামালাং সরলাং
সুস্মিতাং ভূষিতাম্
ধরনীং ভরণীম্
মাতরম্।

poems.title: Vande Mataram (Mother, I bow to thee)
poems.author: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
poems.collection: Vande Mataram, translated by Aurobindo Ghose (1909)
poems.note: Aurobindo Ghose's verse translation, published in Karmayogin, 20 November 1909; it translates the Bengali song above.
poems.text:
Mother, I bow to thee!
Rich with thy hurrying streams,
bright with orchard gleams,
Cool with thy winds of delight,
Dark fields waving Mother of might,
Mother free.

Glory of moonlight dreams,
Over thy branches and lordly streams,
Clad in thy blossoming trees,
Mother, giver of ease
Laughing low and sweet!
Mother I kiss thy feet,
Speaker sweet and low!
Mother, to thee I bow.

Who hath said thou art weak in thy lands,
When the sword flash out in the seventy million hands
And seventy million voices roar
Thy dreadful name from shore to shore?
With many strengths who art mighty and stored,
To thee I call Mother and Lord!
Thou who savest, arise and save!
To her I cry who ever her foe man drove
Back from plain and Sea
And shook herself free.

Thou art wisdom, thou art law,
Thou art heart, our soul, our breath
Thou art love divine, the awe
In our hearts that conquers death.
Thine the strength that nerves the arm,
Thine the beauty, thine the charm.
Every image made divine
In our temples is but thine.

Thou art Durga, Lady and Queen,
With her hands that strike and her swords of sheen,
Thou art Lakshmi lotus-throned,
And the Muse a hundred-toned,
Pure and perfect without peer,
Mother lend thine ear,
Rich with thy hurrying streams,
Bright with thy orchard gleams,
Dark of hue O candid-fair.

In thy soul, with jewelled hair
And thy glorious smile divine,
Loveliest of all earthly lands,
Showering wealth from well-stored hands!
Mother, mother mine!
Mother sweet, I bow to thee,
Mother great and free!
